title.text:
Capstone presentations
and your path from here

objects.text: Can you explain what you built, what it can and cannot do, and what you will learn next?

AI and Data Science Professional  |  Session 24 of 24  |  Module F: Ship it and present
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome to the last session. Over twenty-three sessions you went from a spreadsheet to a tested model, a small app and a fairness audit. Today you learn to present it. You will tell a result as an answer, evidence and limits, write an executive summary, and prepare for the questions a manager asks.

We also list plainly what this course did not cover, and you choose what to learn next.

Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can tell a result as a story with three parts: the answer, the evidence beside a baseline model, and the limits. You can write an executive summary, present to a manager and answer questions on method and risk.

And you can name what this course did not cover, and choose your next free courses and a portfolio plan. There is no code today. The lab is a rehearsal in a Google Sheet, where you plan, time and score each other.

title.text:
Your two hours: concepts
first, then a rehearsal lab

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x2.95_1fc69abc.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: Ideas first. Then you plan and rehearse your talk in a sheet. Then the checks and what you keep.

slides.notes:
We have two hours. The first ten minutes bring back Session 23 and set the question for today. Then forty-five minutes of concepts, with no laptops open: how to tell a result as a story, how to write an executive summary, how to present to a manager, how to keep a portfolio, and what this course left out.

After a ten minute break we open a Google Sheet for a forty-five minute lab. You plan your talk, time a rehearsal, prepare answers to hard questions and score a partner. The last ten minutes are an exit check and what you keep.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What is the difference between data drift and concept drift?
2.  A rule never uses gender, yet it approves 70.3% of women and 52.4% of men. What is going on, and what do you measure?
3.  Name two things that never go into a public GitHub repository.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 23. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. What is the difference between data drift and concept drift?

A good answer is this. In data drift the inputs change after training. In concept drift the link between the inputs and the outcome changes.

Question two. A rule never uses gender, yet it approves 70.3% of women and 52.4% of men. What is going on, and what do you measure?

A good answer is this. A proxy variable (occupation) carries the information. Measure approval and error rates by group and the disparate impact ratio, here 0.745.

Question three. Name two things that never go into a public GitHub repository.

A good answer is this. Personal data such as names, phone numbers or loan records of real people, and passwords, keys or tokens.

If you missed one, check your notes from last session tonight. Now to today.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Capstone. The larger project that ends a course. Yours is a question, data, a model with a baseline model, its limits and a talk.

Executive summary. A short opening paragraph with the answer, the evidence, the main limit and the decision you ask for. A busy reader may read only this.

Limitation. Something your result cannot tell you, such as who the data left out. You say it before you show the result.

Portfolio. A small set of your projects, for example GitHub repositories with a README, that a stranger can open and judge.

Rubric. A marking guide that lists what good work looks like for each criterion. You use it to score your partner.

title.text:
Tell a result as a story in three parts:
the answer, the evidence and the limits

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_38400994.png
objects.alt: Tell a result as a story in three parts: the answer, the evidence and the limits

objects.text: The same story works for any capstone. Put the answer first, so the room knows what the evidence is for.

slides.notes:
Every good result tells a story in three parts. The answer comes first: what you recommend. For our loan model, use it to choose which loans an officer reviews first. The evidence comes next, and it always sits beside a baseline model. Our model finds 43 percent of defaults when it flags about 14 percent of loans.

The limits close the story: fictional data, a fairness check by group, and a person who decides. If one part is missing, the room will not know what to do with your work. What is the answer of your own capstone, in one sentence?

objects.text: Same loans and the same split as Sessions 14 to 17 (logistic regression, 27 columns, decision threshold 0.2). Your Session 16 numbers may differ a little if your model or decision threshold differ.

slides.notes:
This is the evidence we will use for practice, from the Nile Microfinance loans. There are 8,000 loans and 1,004 defaulted, which is 12.6 percent. We held out 2,000 loans, with 251 defaults. The baseline model says repaid every time. It is 87.5 percent accurate and finds no defaults.

Our model at a decision threshold of one half is 89.2 percent accurate, but finds only 51 of the 251 defaults. At a decision threshold of 0.2 it flags 278 loans and finds 108, which is 43.0 percent. The area under the curve is 0.756. These are the same loans, the same split and the same model as Sessions 15 and 16, so your Session 16 numbers may differ a little only if your model or decision threshold differ.

Which row is the story?

title.text:
An accuracy number alone misleads:
show the baseline model beside it

objects.text: The number alone
With the baseline

runs.text: At decision threshold 0.5 the model finds 51 of 251 defaults.

objects.text: Report the baseline, the share of defaults found and the limit in one sentence.

slides.notes:
Here is the trap in every capstone talk. You say the model is 89.2 percent accurate, and it sounds strong. Then a careful person asks what a model that always says repaid would score. The answer is 87.5 percent, so your model is barely ahead. This is the accuracy paradox, and it happens when one answer is much more common.

At a decision threshold of one half, the model finds only 51 of 251 defaults. So give three things in one sentence: the baseline, the share of defaults found, and the limit. What would your capstone baseline be?

title.text:
An executive summary gives the answer,
evidence, limit and request in four sentences

objects.text: An executive summary is the short opening paragraph that a busy reader may read alone. Illustrative example for the loan model:
Answer
Use the model to choose which loans a loan officer reviews first.
Evidence
On 2,000 held-out loans it found 43% of defaults by flagging 14% of loans. The baseline model finds none.
Limit
The data is fictional and 379 loans lack income. We have not tested it after the data changes.
Request
Approve a three month trial where a person decides, with a fairness check by gender each month.

slides.notes:
This is what an executive summary looks like. Four sentences. The answer: use the model to choose which loans an officer reviews first. The evidence: on 2,000 held-out loans it found 43 percent of defaults by flagging 14 percent of loans, while the baseline model finds none. The limit: the data is fictional, 379 loans lack income, and we have not tested it after the data changes.

And the request: approve a three month trial where a person decides, with a fairness check by gender each month. A manager can decide from these four sentences alone. Write the four sentences for your capstone in the lab.

title.text:
A ten-minute talk has five slides:
question, data, evidence, risk and decision

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_dl_segments_11.90x4.25_77a9d991.png
objects.alt: A ten-minute talk has five slides: question, data, evidence, risk and decision

objects.text: Risk: what could go wrong, and who checks. Decision: what you recommend.

slides.notes:
Here is the shape of your ten minute talk. Five slides. Slide one is the question: the decision someone faces, one minute. Slide two is the data: what it covers and what it leaves out, two minutes. Slide three is the evidence, the result beside its baseline, three minutes, the longest.

Slide four is the risk: what could go wrong and who checks, two minutes. Slide five is the decision: what you recommend and the next step, two minutes. Your executive summary becomes your opening sentence. Rehearse with a timer, because most people run long. Which slide will you be tempted to stretch?

objects.text: Start with the answer. One number per slide. Keep the notebook ready for questions.

slides.notes:
A manager has a few minutes and a decision to make. So start with the answer, give one number per slide, and keep the notebook ready for questions. Use the real term, because the manager may hear it again from the data team, and then say what it means.

Recall: of every hundred loans that default, how many we flag. Precision: of every hundred loans we flag, how many really default. The area under the curve is how well the model ranks risky loans above safe ones. A baseline model is the simple rule to beat. The decision threshold is the risk level at which a loan goes to an officer.

And a test set is loans the model never saw. Which term do you tend to use without explaining?

title.text:
Say the limits before the result,
and the room trusts the result

objects.text: Result first

runs.text: Limits arrive in the last minute.
The claim lands before the caveat.

objects.text: Limits first

runs.text: Opens with what the data covers.
Names what the model cannot do.

objects.text: A limit you state loses no marks. A hidden one does.

slides.notes:
Two ways to open. On the left, the result comes first, with the best number. The limits squeeze into the last minute, and the room has already heard the claim, so anything you add sounds like a retreat. On the right you open with what the data covers: eight thousand fictional loans, ten districts, almost three years.

Then you name what the model cannot do. It cannot say why a borrower defaults, and it knows nothing about borrowers who were refused a loan. Then you show the result. People trust a speaker who names the limits first. Try it in your own words in the lab.

What is the biggest limit of your capstone?

title.text:
Three questions on method,
and answers you can give

rows.text: How do you know it works on new loans?
I kept 2,000 loans the model never saw as a test set, and compared the result with a baseline model.
Why that metric and that decision threshold?
Missing a default costs more than reviewing a good loan, so I watch recall. At decision threshold 0.2 it finds 43% of defaults, and about 39 of every 100 flagged loans really default.
This was one split. I would repeat it with k-fold cross-validation and report the range of scores.

slides.notes:
Three questions about method that you should expect. How do you know it works on new loans?

Answer: I kept a test set the model never saw and compared it with a baseline model. Why that metric and that decision threshold?

Because missing a default costs more than reviewing a good loan, so I watch recall. At a decision threshold of 0.2 the model finds 43 percent of defaults, and about 39 of every hundred flagged loans really default. Could it be luck?

Honest answer: this was one split, so I would repeat it with k-fold cross-validation and report the range. An honest answer that names what is not finished is a good answer. Write your three answers in the lab.

title.text:
Three questions on risk: drift,
fairness and data protection

rows.text: What could go wrong once people use it?
The data could drift after training. I would compare each month of inputs with the training period, compare predicted with actual defaults, and set a review date.
Is it fair, and are we allowed to use this data?

I audited approval and error rates by gender: 86.5% of women and 85.6% of men approved. I checked the purpose and data minimisation against the Data Protection and Privacy Act, 2019 (a teaching summary, not legal advice). A person decides.
(Example answer for our fictional lender.) The credit manager owns the model card, and the data protection officer reviews each release.

The data could drift after training, so I compare each month of inputs with the training period, compare predicted with actual defaults, and set a review date. Is it fair, and are we allowed to use this data?

I audited approval rates by gender, 86.5 percent for women and 85.6 percent for men, and I checked purpose and data minimisation against the Data Protection and Privacy Act of 2019. A person decides. And who is responsible?

A portfolio is a small set of your projects that a stranger can open and understand in five minutes. On GitHub that means a few repositories, each laid out like this one. The README comes first. The notebook runs from the top. The model card says what the model is for and where it fails.

The requirements file lets someone repeat your result. The app is optional. The data folder holds generated or public data only, never real customer data, and the gitignore file keeps secrets out. Choose two or three projects you can explain best. What would be the name of your first repository?

slides.notes:
A rubric is a marking guide. Ours has four rows and you score from one to three. Question and evidence: strong work has a one sentence question and every claim points to data. Metric and baseline: a metric chosen for the cost, on unseen data, beside a baseline model.

Limits and fairness: limits first, risks named, groups compared, data duties checked. And clarity: five slides, ten minutes, plain words and one decision. A score of two means partly there. objects.text: Say these gaps yourself, before anyone asks.

slides.notes:
Being honest about gaps is part of being trusted. Seven things this course did not cover, as I understand the session list. Mathematics by hand: you calculated many results by hand, but you did not prove them. Data structures and algorithms: job interview puzzles need separate practice. Big data tools: your data fitted in one notebook.

Paid cloud platforms: you used Colab, GitHub and Streamlit Community Cloud, which have free tiers. Deep learning from scratch: you built a neuron and a small network in numpy, and the pretrained model was optional. Dashboards and business intelligence tools such as Power BI: we named them as hand-over tools but did not teach them.

And production machine learning operations: your app is small, with no container, automated tests or monitoring. Say these gaps yourself before anyone asks. Which gap matters most for your job?

objects.text: Provider estimates at the time of writing. Some are marketing figures. They change.

slides.notes:
Where does this course sit?

It is forty-eight hours. Next to it are provider estimates as listed in late October 2026. They are the providers own estimates, some are marketing figures, and they change, so check each page. The Google crash course is about fifteen hours, Elements of AI about thirty, and a Kaggle Learn micro-course three to five hours.

The DeepLearning dot AI Machine Learning Specialization is about ninety-five hours, the IBM Data Science Professional Certificate about one hundred and seventy-eight, and the Google Data Analytics Certificate over one hundred and eighty. Across data certificates, one hundred and fifty to two hundred and forty hours is often quoted.

So this course gives you a base that later study extends. Which programme will you try next?

title.text:
Your six month path: practice,
depth, portfolio, at 6 hours a week

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_timeline_11.90x4.25_a88a6ee6.png
objects.alt: Your six month path: practice, depth, portfolio, at 6 hours a week

objects.text: 6 h a week for 26 weeks is 156 h.

slides.notes:
Here is a six month path. Months one and two are practice: repeat the labs on new data and finish one Kaggle Learn course. Months three and four are depth: pick one area from the gap list and go further. Months five and six are the portfolio: publish two projects and one app, each with a README.

Choose a weekly budget you can keep. Six hours a week for twenty-six weeks is 156 hours, which is about the low end of the hours often quoted for a data certificate. Four hours a week is also fine, as long as you keep it. What weekly budget will you set?

Where will you use this on Monday?

Four examples. A credit analyst at a bank or SACCO presenting to the monthly credit committee should open with the answer and the baseline model, say the limits first, and show approval rates by group. An officer in a ministry writing a briefing note should write the executive summary in four sentences with one number and its source.

A data officer at an NGO writing a donor report should say what the data covers and leaves out. And an analyst at a retailer should explain recall and precision in plain words, with the cost of a mistake in shillings. Which of these meetings is closest to yours?

title.text: Part 2: rehearsal and feedback

objects.text: Close the slides. Open the sheet.

slides.notes:
That is the end of the ideas. There is no code today. Open a new Google Sheet and call it Presentation plan. You will make tabs as we go: plan, rehearsal, questions, feedback and path. In every task, plan first, then do it, then check your numbers against the table on the screen.

You present to a partner, and your partner scores you with the rubric. Listening to feedback is part of the skill.

title.text:
The lab has five parts, and
you keep a presentation sheet

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_5d225943.png
objects.alt: The lab has five parts, and you keep a presentation sheet

objects.text: Six tasks in 45 minutes. For each task, plan, do it, then check your numbers.

slides.notes:
Here is the map of the lab, in five parts. Part one, plan your five slides with minutes that add up to ten. Part two, rehearse aloud with a timer and record the time of each slide. Part three, prepare three answers: method, metric and risk. Part four, present to a partner for ten minutes and score each other on the four rubric rows, with one comment each.

Part five, write your six month path with a weekly hour budget. The numbers in the first tasks are illustrative, so you can check your formulas. Please do not skip the rehearsal. It is where talks improve.

objects.text: Illustrative scores for the formula check. Your partner fills this in for your talk.

slides.notes:
This is the feedback tab your partner fills in. Four rows from the rubric, a score from one to three, and one comment. Each comment should point to a named slide, and at least one should say what to keep. Here the illustrative scores add up to 11 out of twelve with the SUM formula.

Notice the comments: they are specific. Keep, add, say before. A comment such as good job teaches nothing. When you receive feedback, write it down and do not defend yourself. You can ask a question to understand it. What kind of comment helps you most?

objects.text: If your number differs, find the task that went wrong.

slides.notes:
Use this table as your checkpoint. If one number does not match, call me, because later tasks use earlier ones. The most common cause is a range that includes the header row, or typing minutes where the sheet expects seconds. Your own talk will have different numbers, and that is fine.

These check the formulas on the illustrative data. Find out why it differs. What does it mean if your rehearsal total is under nine minutes?

title.text: Five likely mistakes in the lab and how to fix them

rows.text: In the minutes table: 11 where you expected 10
The minutes add up to more than the plan.
Cut a sentence from the longest slide, then add the minutes again.
Text where a number is expected, such as "70 s".
Type 70 only. Put the unit in the header.
In the feedback tab: 12 where 11 was expected
The range includes the total row, or the header row.
The scores are not separating strong from weak.
Find one thing to improve on each row.
A path with no named course
Without a course and a date, it stays a wish.
Name one course, a start date and the hours a week.

Five problems you may meet. A total of eleven instead of ten means your minutes add up to more than the plan, so cut a sentence from the longest slide. A value error in a time formula usually means text in the cell, such as seventy s, so type the number only.

A sum that includes the total row or the header gives a wrong number, so check the range. If you score everything three, the scores are not helping, so find one improvement on each row. And a path with no named course is a wish. Name the course, the start date and the weekly hours.

title.text:
Exit check: three questions, then
compare with the short answers

rows.text: Which three parts make a result into a story?
The answer, the evidence beside a baseline model, and the limits.
Name two things to say before you show a result.
What the data covers and leaves out, and what the model cannot do. Name the baseline too.
Where do you confirm the terms of a free course?
On the provider page, before you start, because free audit and certificate rules change.

Last, the exit check. Three questions. Write your answers before you look at mine. One, which three parts make a result into a story?

Two, name two things to say before you show a result. Three, where do you confirm the terms of a free course?

The short answers are on the slide. If you got all three, you are ready to present your capstone. This is the end of the course. Choose your first free course today, write the start date in your sheet, and send it to me. Thank you for twenty-four sessions of hard work.
